\chapter{When Bien Is Not True --- Calm, Ill, Content, Busy, Sad}
\label{ch:como-estoy}
\hlchaptermodality{304}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can answer how I am honestly in Spanish: calm, ill, content, busy or sad, in the right form for who is speaking.}

Complete ES-C304-triste: give all five answers, switching the four that take -o/-a and leaving the one that ends in -e alone.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tranquilo]{tranquilo — a sea with no wind on it}

\label{lesson:ES-C304-tranquilo}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{tranquilo} — \textquotedblleft{}calm.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{tranquillus} was, before anything else, a word for \textbf{water}: a sea or a lake with no wind moving across it. Flat, and therefore safe to cross.

English borrowed it whole and kept the picture, whether or not anybody notices it: \emph{tranquil}, \emph{tranquillity}.

It is the most-used answer in this chapter after \emph{bien}, and it does something the others do not — said to somebody else, \emph{tranquilo} means \textquotedblleft{}take it easy,\textquotedblright{} a whole sentence in one word.

A man says \emph{tranquilo}; a woman says \emph{tranquila}. You met that \emph{-o}/\emph{-a} switch in \emph{bueno} and \emph{buena}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can answer the wellbeing question with something other than \emph{bien}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tranquilo}
  \item \emph{tranquila}
  \item \emph{tranquilo, gracias}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{tranquillus} describe first? (Water with no wind on it.) And what does a woman say? (\emph{Tranquila}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[enfermo]{enfermo — not firm}

\label{lesson:ES-C304-enfermo}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{enfermo} — \textquotedblleft{}ill.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{infirmus} is \emph{in-} (\textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{firmus} (\textquotedblleft{}firm, steady\textquotedblright{}). Illness named as \textbf{the loss of steadiness} — not pain, not fever, just the going of the thing that held you up.

English borrowed it twice and kept the shape both times: \emph{infirm}, and the \emph{infirmary} where the not-firm are put.

\emph{Enfermo} is the strong one in this chapter. You already have \emph{la fiebre} and \emph{el dolor}; this is the word for the state they belong to. And \emph{la enfermera} — the nurse — is built straight off it: the one who attends the not-firm.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two honest answers now, and one of them explains a word you already had.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{enfermo}
  \item \emph{enferma}
  \item \emph{enfermo — la enfermera, por favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Take \emph{infirmus} apart. (\emph{In-} not, \emph{firmus} firm.) Which word you already knew is built on it? (\emph{La enfermera}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[contento]{contento — held together}

\label{lesson:ES-C304-contento}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{contento} — \textquotedblleft{}happy,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}content.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{contentus} is the past participle of \emph{continere}, \textquotedblleft{}to hold together\textquotedblright{} — \emph{con-} plus \emph{tenere}, \textquotedblleft{}to hold.\textquotedblright{} So \emph{contento} is literally \textbf{held together}.

English took the verb as \emph{contain} and the participle as \emph{content}, and kept the double life: a \emph{container} holds things; a \emph{contented} person is held.

That is a quieter word than \textquotedblleft{}happy.\textquotedblright{} It does not claim delight. It claims that nothing is falling apart — which, next to \emph{tranquilo} and \emph{enfermo}, is exactly the right register for answering a stranger.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three answers: worn out, not firm, and held together.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{contento}
  \item \emph{contenta}
  \item \emph{contento, gracias}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{continere} mean? (To hold together.) So what is a \emph{contento} person, literally? (Held together.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ocupado]{ocupado — seized}

\label{lesson:ES-C304-ocupado}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ocupado} — \textquotedblleft{}busy.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{occupare} meant \textbf{to seize}, to take possession of — an army occupies ground. English kept it exactly: to \emph{occupy}, and an \emph{occupation}.

So \emph{ocupado} does not say \textquotedblleft{}I have a lot on.\textquotedblright{} It says \textbf{something has taken hold of me}. The work is the one doing the grabbing.

It is also the word on a lavatory door, and what a Spanish phone line is when it is busy — the seat and the line are both \emph{seized}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four honest answers, and one of them is written on doors.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ocupado}
  \item \emph{ocupada}
  \item \emph{lo siento — ocupado}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{occupare} mean? (To seize.) So who is doing the seizing when you are \emph{ocupado}? (The work.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[triste]{triste — the one word that does not change}

\label{lesson:ES-C304-triste}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{triste} — \textquotedblleft{}sad.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{tristis} was wider than the English word. It covered \emph{grim}, \emph{harsh}, \emph{severe} — a \emph{tristis} judge was a stern one — and only later settled onto sorrow. French carried the softer end into \emph{tristesse}, which English borrowed without translating.

Here is the thing worth noticing, and it is a rule you have been shown four times now without it being named: \emph{tranquilo} becomes \emph{tranquila}, \emph{contento} becomes \emph{contenta}, \emph{ocupado} becomes \emph{ocupada}. \textbf{Triste does not move.}

Words ending in \emph{-e} have one form for everybody. That is not an exception to the \emph{-o}/\emph{-a} switch; it is the other half of it, and it costs you nothing to learn because there is nothing to change.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five answers — and the fifth quietly teaches the limit of the \emph{-o}/\emph{-a} rule.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{triste}
  \item \emph{triste, gracias}
  \item \emph{contento — contenta — triste}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Did \emph{tristis} only mean sad? (No — grim and harsh too.) And why does \emph{triste} not change for a woman? (It ends in \emph{-e}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
